comments.name: Bear
comments.body: I understand cosmetic surgery as an individual choice— and for people in the media I can only imagine the pressure. But what bothers me about it is that it changes the playing field for everyone else. I am 50, and increasingly it feels like plastic surgery and injections are the norm- and not embracing them is some sort of counter cultural rebellion. The other day I listened to a podcast about Korean standards of beauty and it said that in Korea it is a woman’s obligation to her family to look as pretty as possible and if surgery is necessary than they are expected to do it! I reject this. I will not change my face because I want my kids to see me as a mind and soul, not as an upkeep project. I think of the less financially-secure people in my community who are running up debt on the only plastic surgeons they can afford on credit and it just depresses me. Increasingly, staying young-looking is a sign of wealth and status- and I do not want to participate in a cultural trend that I think is broadly making people’s lives worse. You should not need tens of thousands of dollars (not to mention pain and recovery) to have a “normal face”. So I will walk around with my wrinkles and hope it makes other people feel better about theirs. My face does not need to be renovated.

I don’t think it’s about the male glaze only, it’s about our own glaze and expectations for ourselves as we try to keep ourselves in the game of life.  It’s about being able to continue working and making money, whether you are in front of a camera, or sitting in a research lab behind closed doors.  It’s also about more “less invasive” ways to keep our skin healthy and glowing (from amazing moisturizers to full-on plastic surgery) - because we as women (and men) want it and like it.  At the end of the day, it’s not about men looking at us, it’s about us looking at us.  Oh BTW, I’m seeing that more men are caring about how they look too, and going to the dermatologist to care for their skin.  No human, male or female, is immune to the passage of time or the desire to look good for ourselves.  I live in NYC, so I see gorgeous people everyday, male/female, older and young.  I love to see how people put themselves together as they go about their day commuting to work or school.  People are really stylish, even in the most simplest of clothing (I’m talking about really cool T-shirts and jeans).  To me that is what makes us interesting and attractive to look at, our sense of style, the way our health shines through, whether someone got a filler or just goes sans makeup.  I just love people watching.

I still recall a conversation I had in the early 80s with a couple of Reaganite financial planners (which was then an up-and-coming profession).  Their view was that parents were foolish to save while their children were young and then use the proceeds to pay for college education.  Better, they argued, to invest the money for themselves and let their children borrow to cover college costs, then pay back the loans as they got jobs and their incomes grew.

Fast forward to 2008, when those chickens came home to roost.  Whole generations now owed huge debts that had accumulated, ruining their credit scores and preventing them from buying a first house.  In the meantime, colleges had increased programs and tuition beyond the rate of inflation because it was easy to push the costs off on students, who themselves were pushing the debt off to the future.  And seeing that there wasn't any pushback from their voters (the parents of these students), state legislatures reduced supports for public higher education, thereby increasing further the need to raise tuition and increase loan amounts.  

I have often wished I could go back and have a conversation with those Reaganite financial planners, armed with the experience of the past 40 years and the dreadful results that befell students, colleges, and our nation.

Good conversation but it didn’t get to the pin that pricks the bubble: AI is not delivering the ROI it’s been selling to enterprise and worse, its use degrades organizational capacity. 

The first is because LLMs turn out to work extremely well but only in a tiny fraction of the actual value-generating range of human economic life: e.g., software coding, which as a symbolically-consistent system LLMs can accelerate productivity significantly; most other domains of value production are far more messy and semantic, requiring social relations, human judgment, human legitimation, human:human interaction, physical manipulation etc. AI will only deliver ROI in this class of tasks when entire workflows and society-wide economic processes are reengineered. It will happen, but long after the bubble realizes it’s mispriced how many enterprises will clamp down on spending (90% of enterprise AI pilots aren’t moving out of pilot).

Second, as AI increasingly stands in for human cognition it degrades the judgment and agential capacity of the humans involved. Enterprises will not sacrifice their competitiveness and talent for this tradeoff, and this effect is just hitting the literature now. This is a massive problem and represents a huge misjudgment of how AI would aid human life; it does and can, but only in very niche and narrowly-defined ways.

The AI bubble cannot survive either of these realities. The capital markets haven’t priced them in, but they will soon enough.

comments.name: Hari Prasad

Basil (Tulsi) leaves are placed in water and food containers to protect them: People stay indoors during the peak (Sutak), chant protective mantras, and take a ritual bath in holy rivers or at home once the eclipse ends to purify themselves. Pregnant women take extra precautions to protect the unborn child. In Chinese tradition, a celestial dragon or monster is attempting to devour the Sun or Moon. People rushed outside to bang drums, crash pots, beat gongs, and shout loudly at the sky.The primary goal of the noise was to scare away the hungry dragon so it would spit out the Sun or Moon, restoring light to the world. In Mesopotamia, eclipses were treated as precise, terrifying divine warnings sent by the gods regarding the fate of the state and specifically the king.

My bona fides: Saw a total solar eclipse on the Big Island of Hawaii in 1991. It was cloudy, so we took off on the coastal highway to find a clear patch of sky. At the very last moment, the clouds parted and the spectacle began. And it was a spectacle! Hundreds of lucky cars found parking on the sides of the road. At totality people cheering, shouting and the blaring of conch shell trumpets. It really was a type of party, but with no unwanted music, serenity or a lecture. Just awe in every sense. Such awe that swept us off of the planet to the astonishing workings of our solar system. And hundreds of people defying every-day gravity right along with us.

The fullness of eclipse totality is something which must be experienced, not lectured about. It's much too fleeting. Lectures can happen later.

Many years ago, I was in grad school.  Studying Greek and Latin.  And one of my assignments was--

--read the Iliad.

And week by week, I would report to my advisor on Book I.  Then Book II.  And so on, till I finished Book XXIV.  

Guess what?  I would defer the task till the night before.  Then pull an all-nighter.  Oh joy! 

And there I'd sit, going over those hundreds of hexameters.  In Greek.  And the hours went plodding by--

--till I'd notice a slight grayness in the sky.  Oh so slight!  But the gray was growing and growing--

--till all of a sudden, a golden beam of sunlight fell across my text of Homer.  And I swear! 

--again and again, it was as if invisible trumpets were sounding an inaudible fanfare.  Another day!  The sun in all his glowing majesty was rising in the east--

--"as a strong man rejoiceth to run a race" as it says in the Psalms.  

Oh how right you are!  So many things are worthy of awe.  The Grand Canyon (which we saw years ago).  Glaciers on the coast of Alaska (which we saw a few weeks ago).  

And this--

--the scene between Achilles and King Priam at the end of the Iliad.  I read this (in the early hours of the morning)--

--and I told myself--

--you will never in all your life read anything more sublime, more moving and wonderful.

A tiny measure of forgiveness, of reconciliation--

--between two bitter and avowed enemies!  It happens--

--and when it does! 

--we stand there, looking on.  Awestruck. 

Thanks, NYT

Depending on the kind of event, there could be things that you are supposed to know about someone, or that they will be pleased if you know.  So suppose the event involves faculty at a college, and you look up what someone wrote a book about.  I don't see why it is bad to check that in advance so you go in knowing that.

I know someone who, before a large family event, asks his sister to remind him what the names of some of his relatives' spouses are, or for that matter some of his relatives.  I suppose you could probably use social media, or maybe Google, for the same purpose.

But I agree with another commenter that probably you don't want to tell the person how you know this information, information that they think you don't, or shouldn't, have to look up.

The purpose in these cases is to correct a failing that the searcher has, or at least to give them information that it would be totally normal for them to have, and in the case of the book would lead to pleasant and productive conversation.  But as to the idea of "creepy," I think it's interesting.  I can't fully explain why, but I don't think the kids are coming from nowhere.  If the search is excessively thorough and exhaustive, I think it would go beyond the bounds of what we expect in a normal social situation.  Not sure if this is ethics or social q's.  I think of Robert De Niro subjecting the prospective son-in-law to a lie detector test.  "Excessively intrusive" comes to mind.

comments.name: A Human

The Googling is not unethical. Just as, to paraphrase Agatha Christie, in a public place, if someone is not speaking in hushed voices, one might reasonably assume they are prepared to be overheard, if someone posts something online, for all to see, one must assume they are prepared for everyone to see it. It’s off-putting how much the internet knows about people, but it’s not wrong to use that information. If you were hacking into their computer’s photo library or something, that would be different. The real question is: are you willing to stand the awkwardness of someone possibly realising that you’ve Googled them? and would that realisation damage future social discourse? Frankly, I am of the mind that if someone is made uncomfortable by something that one does regularly, it’s not especially smart to spend a lot of time around them (though if these are people from work, there may be little choice in that matter) anyway, but I’m not a person to ask for social advice. 

Also, there might be some trouble making certain that the things that pop up on Google are even the right person. If you Google “John Smith” chances are good that NONE of the things that come up will be the person you are looking for. I assume that you have some system for verifying this (probably there’s some way to tell where somebody lives by looking at their social media).

In June 1989, I was in Shanghai. After 06/04, Mayor Zhu gave a TV speech, which was not common back then. He basically said he would take necessary means to keep the city running. He did not parrot anybody, or sounded strident. I was impressed. Having left for the US, I did not follow China as closely as I wished. 

Zhu was smart, and attended China's MIT. Back then one who graduated from primary school was regarded as an intellectual. No kidding. He joined the party at the time of its rise to power. In 1958, he suffered prosecution, losing his party membership for two decades.

For me, he was famous for four things. First, he started the reform in Shanghai, the most important city in China. Second, he tackled the toughest problem in the transition to a market economy: privatization, and offended those who lost jobs. Third, he played the leading role in getting China into the WTO, which was no easy job, since both Chinese and Americans had to make compromises. Looking back, China has benefited from the integration into the world economy. Finally, he claimed to be incorruptible and seemed to be so. He was eloquent and straightforward, which is rare for Chinese politicians or for that matters, any politicians. 

Post-Mao China has had several capable leaders, despite their different styles. While not number one, Zhu was among them. It cannot go unnoticed that they all lived past 90. President Hu is about 84, although he looks a bit frail.

Mr. Bradsher’s obituary brought back my only encounter with the late Mr. Zu:

On the evening of April 7, 1999 (U.S. time), during his official visit to Washington, D.C., at Washington Hilton on the 16th street where he stayed, Mr. Zhu met with hundreds of Chinese students from 20 U.S. states. I was one of them. After a long day of talks with US officials, at 10 pm, Mr. Zhu enters the hall, with a thunderous applause, the audience plead him to sit down before speaking. Mr. Zhu, tired but spirited, says, ”I think standing suits the occasion and me.” He spares the audience the complexity of US-China relations but elaborates on his delegation’s visits to multiple American states. “Facing the American people directly at every stop to enhance mutual understanding, foster cooperation, and clarify China's stance is far more important than simply signing a few agreements!” Mr. Zhu then shifts the subject and turns to the audience itself. “I know how hard to establish a foothold abroad. Please accept my heartfelt respect for your resilience and hard work.” I was moved.

Mr. Zhu’s impromptu speech, candid, with empathy and a wry sense of humor, a cherished memory of mine, serves as a timely but often neglected reminder, that a good statesman diffuses hostilities and enhances similarities among geopolitical peers.

comments.name: Steve Johnson

Due to some extraordinary circumstances, I ended up in Shanghai in 1989 during the protest when Zhu Rongji was mayor. He was a centrist—a real rarity at the time. Deng Xiaoping had officially semi retired, Li Peng represented the hardliners, and Zhao Ziyang represented the liberal faction of the Chinese Communist Party.
After Tiananmen, Zhu voiced his support for the central government in Beijing. The protests in Shanghai eventually ebbed, partly because a well-respected technocrat had thrown his weight behind the government to maintain stability.
He was later promoted to Beijing alongside Jiang Zemin who was the party leader of Shanghai by Deng Xiaoping to move the country past the tragic legacy of Tiananmen. This move ushered in decades of pragmatic, non-ideological economic policy.
Deng was a pragmatist and a visionary, but Zhu was extraordinary. It was exceptionally rare for a centrist politician in China to not only survive the political system, but to rise as one of its core leaders and help build modern China.

RIP.

For most complex tasks, AI appears to be much more powerful as a force multiplier for people who already know what good work looks like. AI dramatically expands execution capacity: it can search, calculate, draft, code, reconcile data, construct models, produce alternatives, and increasingly dispatch agents through multi-step workflows. But someone still has to decide what the task really is, specify it intelligently, recognize when the output is wrong, identify omitted considerations, resolve contradictions, and know when an apparently plausible answer is economically, legally, technically, or strategically absurd. Those are precisely the things that domain knowledge supplies.

Mr. Wardika deserves every bit of this attention, and one of the most inspiring things about Bali is that he is not alone.

Across this island, there are role models refusing to accept environmental loss as inevitable. Sungai Watch’s river warriors are hauling extraordinary amounts of plastic from Bali’s waterways before it reaches the sea. Bye Bye Plastic Bags grew from two young Balinese sisters saying enough into a movement against single-use plastic. Begawan Foundation has spent decades working to bring the critically endangered Bali Starling back from the edge of extinction. And now Wayan Wardika is quite literally bringing back the light.

These efforts address different problems—fireflies, birds, rivers, plastic, farming—but together they tell a much bigger and more hopeful story about Bali: restoration is possible when people decide that what has been lost is worth fighting to bring back.

I would love to see The New York Times tell more of these stories. Bali has many environmental heroes, and the world could learn a great deal from them.

The therapist’s response doesn’t discuss how the brother might be told that he’s not being invited to family gatherings until he’s made repairs… That’s a hugely important piece of this conversation and likely must precede any of the opportunities for the mother to listen to the brother.  

It would be helpful to see the therapist’s advice for this particular conversation because it could easily go south and become a judgmental/lecturing style dialogue that the therapist advises avoiding.  

It also seems, assuming that the brother and the sister once had a good relationship (and if not that would be important to know as well because it could be a part of this dynamic ) that if the brother is redeemable through the listening/loving from the mother, then he likely would experience and share in the grief of knowing that his views had alienated his (presumptively) beloved sister, and disrupted the family - which could also be a powerful motivator and also represent some kind nod to the hardline position of indignation as well, which would be entirely appropriate within a family to find some way to express.

Listening and loving alone doesn’t seem to have enough of an edge to it to open his eyes emphatically to the notion that he’s becoming the root cause of something quite drastic and family-changing.

comments.name: Sacha
comments.body:
I find racism repulsing and sympathize with the sister and her family, especially as I'm myself part of a stigmatized minority.
Still, since it's a therapy column, Lori should have mentioned that the son is almost certainly going to feel that the mother is choosing his sister over him because she loves her more. He might very well decide to cut ties entirely with his parents.
By the way, is there a father around? Shouldn't he be part of the decision?
I know only one family who was in a similar situation, so it's not much of a sample, but still a cautionary tale. The sister had good reason to resent her brother and pressured her parents into excluding him from family gatherings. A few years later, she changed her mind because she missed her brother and wanted the children they had both had in between to be close. But now, he feels wary and mostly avoids his family. Some  decisions cannot be reversed.
I'm not saying the sister and mother would be ethically wrong to exclude the racist brother from family gatherings, but I think that for their own sakes, they should make sure to consider the consequences carefully, including for themselves. What if, for instance, the parents need help as they age and the sister isn't able, or willing, to care for them alone?

comments.body:
As an old Freudian I can't help thinking that something is missing from Lori's compassionate and intelligent response. Both children seem to have very [pardon the expression] black-and-white reactions to this dilemma: either you're with me or against me. According to the LW's letter they seem determined to punish the mother [yeah, where is the dad in this? MIA?] So I think an old thread of sibling resentment--even rage--you favor him more than me, you favor her more than me-- runs through this family schism that the LW isn't recognizing. As a parent myself, I identify with the LW's agony that her children don't and won't get along. Few parents want to own up to that. 

As one commenter noted, the son's active racism might explain why he sought  a source of rage to bond with--and punish his birth family with. The daughter won't reconcile with her brother at all. 

I agree that firm boundaries and adjustments about family gatherings need to be made now. But I also think LW would benefit by compassionate help to her work through her inability to deal with her childrens' resentment, hurt, and rage.

For a long time, I worked with trauma victims, and something that hurt and angered them is not only how their pain is ignored and undertreated and promising treatments shelved, but how the general public, including the arts, are often more fascinated with the perpetrators than their victims. 
And even if their stories appear in movies, it often feels wrong, because filmmakers didn't care enough to research the issue, and shy away from the pain of it.
This one is different.
And yes, it's hard to watch, because it should be - sexual abuse is terrible and wrong, and if a movie treats it in a lighthearted way, it's a bad one.
Schindler's List isn't an easy watch either, because it shouldn't be.
There's only a handful of these movies (Hitchcock's 'Marnie' is another) that can actually be used to teach psychologists, doctors, law enforcement, social workers, how trauma really looks and feels to those experiencing it, for them to try to grasp what is unimaginable to most and still happens to many - this is one of them.
Go watch it. 
(Survivors need to be mindful how much of it they can tolerate, but most feel very seen after watching, in my experience)

comments.name: Nogi Ichida
comments.body:
Zhu reminds me of Ōkubo Toshimichi (大久保利通), the Japanese statesman of the Meiji era. Born a samurai, Ōkubo became a stunning reformist who helped abolish the han system and dismantle the privileges of the samurai class in order to modernize Japan. He was eventually assassinated by former samurai, but he and Zhu shared a similar vision and character during periods of profound historical change.

Both Zhu and Ōkubo faced resistance from established interests in their respective countries, including serious political pressure and death threats. Yet their work eventually materialized, for better or worse. Both were technocrats who mastered the difficult balance between liberalizing the economic system and maintaining the political legitimacy of the ruling establishment (Tenno in Japan and CPC in China).

Both helped pave the way for modernization while accepting enormous political backlash and social pain.

The Western perception of Zhu as a reformer who embraced many liberal economic policies also has to be understood in its historical context. China desperately needed Western technology, capital, and access to global markets at the time. China was far from being viewed as a threat; it was largely seen as an opportunity.

Zhu will be remembered by many who benefited from that era. Whatever the caveats, his reforms cemented the foundation of Chinese state capitalism.

I will share a personal observation from 8 April 2024 for folks in the path of totality:

Do not fuss over optimizing/chasing for clear skies. It is far far better to experience 100% totality under a thick deck of clouds than it is to experience 99% totality under clear skies.  That's what a stark difference that last 1% makes, a least if you're away from street and building lights.
 
Experiencing 100% totality under a thick deck of clouds (1) yields a much more profoundly freaky response from fauna of all kinds if you manage to be away from urban/suburban street and building lights, (2) it gets way darker than even with clear skies, and (3) the flashing that is part of the entering/exiting 100% totality is much more emphatic (though it can't be captured on camera) through a cloud deck, like Doomsday, something lost in clear skies. 

I was lucky to have caught an astrophysicist's comments on this very thing the day before the 2024 event. Journalists never cover the cloudy version of a total eclipse. In some respects, it's much more sensorily unnerving.
